headline: An AI Canvas Talks a Path Tracer Into Existence
lede: Omma, the AI canvas built by Spline, Inc., generated a functioning WebGPU path tracer inside a browser through nothing more than a user's conversational prompts. The demo — posted to Omma's own account — includes physically based rendering materials, depth-of-field blur, and an in-progress neural denoiser. It is a striking marker of how far AI code generation has advanced in technically demanding domains.
body:
**Path tracing** is the gold standard for photorealistic light simulation in film and VFX: it fires thousands of random rays per pixel, tracks every light bounce, and averages the results to simulate the full rendering equation — global illumination, caustics, soft shadows, and all. Making it run interactively in a browser has, until very recently, been impractical. What the Omma demo shows is not a pre-built product feature but something more instructive: a user described scene settings in plain English across several iterative chat sessions, and the AI wrote and refined the renderer in response. The session list visible in the OCR includes titles like “WebGPU neural denoiser impl” and “PT + Controls” — scaffolding assembled conversation by conversation, a practice sometimes called *vibe coding*.

The enabling technology is **WebGPU**, the W3C successor to WebGL, which exposes *compute shaders* — general-purpose GPU programs — directly in the browser. WebGL, dating to the OpenGL ES era, had no such primitive; workloads as parallel as path tracing required a native app or a game-engine plugin. WebGPU reached near-universal coverage across Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge by early 2026, with published benchmarks showing roughly 10–15× improvements in compute-heavy workloads over its predecessor. A path tracer is almost entirely GPU compute — millions of ray-triangle intersection tests per frame — making WebGPU's compute tier the critical unlock.

A path tracer's realism rests on two pillars: the *BRDF* (Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function) that governs how light scatters off surfaces, and a denoiser that makes the noisy image usable before it has statistically converged. *PBR* (Physically Based Rendering) standardises the BRDF side around a metallic-roughness workflow — the same material parameters used by *glTF*, Unity (U), and Unreal Engine — so a renderer that “supports PBR” can consume assets from standard pipelines without conversion. The denoiser problem is harder: path-traced images converge slowly (error halves only when sample count quadruples), so a *neural denoiser* — a small CNN trained on paired noisy and clean images — reconstructs a usable frame from as few as one sample per pixel, using surface normals and albedo buffers as guidance.

Omma launched in public beta in March 2026 as Spline’s second product. Where Spline was a browser-based 3D design tool with more than three million users, Omma replaces the manual canvas with parallel AI agents handling code generation, 3D-mesh synthesis, and image generation simultaneously, outputting deployable apps that run natively on WebGPU. Prior open-source web path tracers — notably *strahl* by Simon Stucki and Philipp Ackermann, presented at ACM Web3D 2024, and Georgi Nikolov’s *webgpu-raytracer* — demonstrate what a human-authored WebGPU path tracer looks like. The interesting question the Omma demo raises is how close to those baselines the LLM-generated code actually gets.

Some skepticism is warranted. The tweet says Omma “built” the path tracer and that it “supports PBR” — both claims that need qualification. A path tracer that truly supports PBR must implement an energy-conserving microfacet BRDF; a simplified approximation that looks plausible at a specific camera angle would overstate the result. Likewise, the “neural denoiser” may in practice be a classical *à-trous wavelet* spatial filter — a simpler non-neural technique that a language model is likelier to generate correctly. None of this is verifiable from a screenshot. What is verifiable is that Omma can assemble the scaffolding for a credible path tracer through conversation alone — a meaningful shift from what AI coding assistants could manage eighteen months ago.

concepts.definition: A photorealistic rendering technique that simulates light by firing thousands of random rays per pixel, following each ray as it bounces off surfaces, and averaging the results to solve the full rendering equation. It produces physically correct global illumination — including indirect light, caustics, and soft shadows — but converges slowly, making real-time use without denoising impractical.

A development practice, coined by Andrej Karpathy in 2025, in which a programmer describes intent in plain language and iterates on code generated by an AI assistant rather than writing the code directly. The term captures the conversational, impressionistic quality of the workflow — closer to directing than programming.

The W3C standard that gives browser-based code direct access to modern GPU hardware — Direct3D 12, Metal, and Vulkan — rather than routing through the older OpenGL ES abstraction. Its key addition over WebGL is compute shaders, enabling general-purpose GPU programming (path tracing, neural inference, physics) directly in the browser.

A shading model that simulates how light physically interacts with surfaces using measured material properties — primarily albedo (base colour), metallic (conductor vs. dielectric), and roughness (microsurface detail). Because it models energy conservation, it produces consistent-looking results under any lighting condition and is the standard in real-time engines and offline renderers alike.

GPU programs that run outside the fixed graphics pipeline, enabling arbitrary parallel computation on GPU hardware. Compute shaders are what make WebGPU suitable for workloads like path tracing, physics simulation, and neural inference inside a browser — tasks that were effectively impossible in WebGL, which lacked the primitive.

The mathematical function that describes how much light is reflected from a surface in a given outgoing direction for a specific incoming direction. A physically correct BRDF must conserve energy — it cannot reflect more light than it receives. The GGX/Trowbridge-Reitz microfacet BRDF is the industry standard for PBR shading.

A small convolutional neural network trained to reconstruct a clean rendered image from a very noisy one — typically produced at one sample per pixel. It is guided by auxiliary buffers (surface normals, albedo, depth) that convey scene geometry independent of the lighting noise. Intel’s OIDN and NVIDIA’s OptiX Denoiser are the leading implementations; oidn-web ports OIDN to WebGPU via TensorFlow.js.

A classical (non-neural) spatial denoising filter applied to rendered images. It performs a series of progressively scaled blurs that smooth out Monte Carlo noise while preserving edges by weighting samples by their surface normal and albedo similarity. Cheaper to run than a neural denoiser but less effective at very low sample counts.

An open 3D asset format standard maintained by the Khronos Group, sometimes called the “JPEG of 3D.” It stores geometry, textures, and PBR material parameters (albedo, metallic, roughness, normal maps) in a single transferable file, making it the de facto interchange format for web and mobile 3D pipelines.

The dominant PBR parameter scheme, used by glTF, Unity, Unreal Engine, and most real-time engines. Two scalar values — metallic (0 = dielectric like plastic or wood, 1 = conductor like gold or copper) and roughness (0 = perfect mirror specular, 1 = fully diffuse) — combined with a base colour define how the surface reflects light.

repos.summary: strahl is an open-source, browser-based path tracer built on WebGPU and the OpenPBR material standard, published at ACM Web3D 2024 by Simon Stucki and Philipp Ackermann. It is one of the earliest peer-reviewed WebGPU path tracers and demonstrates physically correct global illumination with standard PBR materials. It serves as a useful human-authored baseline against which AI-generated WebGPU renderers can be compared.

A real-time WebGPU path tracer by Georgi Nikolov that includes both spatial and temporal denoising passes. It demonstrates that interactive path tracing at usable quality is achievable in the browser with a carefully written WGSL implementation, achieving roughly 80fps at one sample per pixel with denoising. It offers a practical reference point for evaluating the correctness and performance of LLM-generated equivalents.

fact_check: The tweet’s framing that Omma “built” the path tracer conflates Omma’s AI generating code in response to user prompts with Omma shipping a renderer as a product feature. The claim that the renderer “supports PBR materials” cannot be verified from a screenshot: a rigorous PBR implementation requires an energy-conserving microfacet BRDF, and a language model may generate a plausible-looking approximation that fails that test. Similarly, the “neural denoiser” shown in the session list may be a classical spatial filter rather than a CNN-based denoiser — the distinction matters for the technical accuracy of the claim. None of these are definitive refutations, but they prevent the claims from being taken at face value without access to the generated source code.
